newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Yakovlev still eyeing Fokker.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Yakovlev still eyeing Fokker.

text.p: Russian plane-maker Yakovlev said on Tuesday it still wanted to buy bankrupt Dutch company Fokker NV and was trying to put together a Russian consortium to do so.
Arkady Gurtovoi, vice-president of Aviatsionnaya Korporatsiya Yakovlev, told Reuters Yakovlev planned to line up several Russian plane-makers for the 370 million guilder deal.
Gurtovoi declined to say who was involved, but said Yakovlev had close contacts with defence aviation group Sukhoi.
Officials at Otdelniye Konstruktorskoye Byuro imeni Sukhova (Sukhoi) were not availiable for comment.
"We are discussing possibilities of buying Fokker and we do not see serious obstacles to this. But the process is very complicated," Gurtovoi said.

Last December four Russian aircraft makers agreed to work together to produce civil planes and helicopters. Yakovlev, Tupolev, Sukhoi and helicopter producer Mil set up a financial-industrial group to carry out the project.
Yakovlev is interested in Fokker to shore up its position in the Russian short-range plane market, of which it wants 25-30 percent by the year 2000.

The company used to be the Soviet Union's foremost designer of military aircraft and still designs naval fighter planes. It also designs passenger aircraft and produced the short-range Yak-40 and Yak-42 models.

Gurtovoi said Yakovlev was cutting its staff of engineers and workers because of a general crisis in the industry. Yakovlev itself has serious financial problems because of unpaid debts from another aviation plant.
It is not clear how Yakovlev would fund a purchase of Fokker, but it has said it will buy the Dutch company without Russian government financial backing if necessary.
"Until the Dutch actually reject us we will continue to work on this project," chief designer Alexander Dondukov said recently.
South Korea's Samsung Aerospace had been the principal candidate to take over Fokker, which went bankrupt in March 1996, but dropped its bid at the end of last year.
The Malaysian government and Saudi Prince al-Waleed bin Talal have both expressed interest in rescuing the company.
